title: Brahma Falls at Krishna's Feet
story:
To Brahma, only a moment had passed. In Vrindavan, a year.

When the creator came back to look for the calves and boys he had hidden away, he found them exactly where they had always been — playing on the sandbank, tending their calves, running home at dusk to mothers who held them as though they had been gone a long while. The cows hurried from their pens at the sound of lowing, and the calves ran to them, and the whole herd went about its evening as if nothing had ever disturbed it. And the love in those homes — the verses say it had grown deeper than before. The cowherd men and women doted on their children with a tenderness that surprised even themselves, and no one could have said why.

Brahma could not tell the difference between what he had hidden and what he saw now. The boys he had carried off — where were they? And these here, who were they? He stood a long while turning it over, and the more he thought the less he understood. He reached for the very power of illusion that had hidden the children in the first place, and tried to use it again — and the illusion merely looked back at him. It was, the verses say, like a firefly's light at noon, or a darkness trying to settle in the mist of a morning that is already gone.

Then, before his eyes, the children changed. Every cowherd boy on the sandbank appeared no longer as a boy but as a four-armed form, holding a conch and a discus, a mace and a lotus. On each chest shone the shrivatsa mark, and on each arm glinted armlets and bracelets, and from head to foot each form was draped in garlands of fresh tulsi leaves. Each face smiled like moonlight, with a sidelong glance full of kindness, and each form was pure being, pure knowledge, and pure, endless joy. Around them, the verses say, stood all the worlds and all the powers that move them, from the first gods down to the last blade of grass, and every one of them in its own form. Where a crowd of village children had been playing, there now stood an endless company of the Lord himself — and Brahma, who had made the universe, stood speechless before it.

Brahma's senses stood still. The verses say the eleven doors of his perception froze where they were, and he could do nothing but look, unable to say what he was seeing. It was too much for him, and then it was hidden — for Krishna saw what was happening, and gently, as one draws a curtain, he covered Brahma's sight. When the creator opened his eyes again, it was like a man waking from the dead. The vision was gone. He looked around, and there was the ordinary world, men and animals sitting together with no sign of their natural enmity. And there, before him, stood a small boy with a morsel of food in his hand, searching for his friends exactly as he had been searching before, playing the part of a cowherd child as if nothing at all had happened.

Brahma came down from his swan and threw himself on the ground like a golden rod. He touched Krishna's feet with the tips of his four crowns, and he bathed them with his tears.
reflection: Brahma came to test, and found himself tested. The vision of countless four-armed forms is overwhelming, but what finally undoes him is the plainness that follows it — a child with a morsel of food, looking for his friends. Krishna's true hiding place, the story suggests, is not the spectacle but the ordinary.
next_story_tease: But Brahma had not yet finished speaking.
hero_scene: Brahma, the four-headed creator, fallen to the ground like a golden rod before the boy Krishna, touching his feet with the tips of his four crowns while tears of joy stream from his eyes.
